The winners of annual awards given out by ASCAP for the year’s most outstanding music writing and broadcasts include biographies of film composers John Williams and Bernard Herrmann , as well as a documentary about cult R&B artist Swamp Dogg, liner notes for an archival release from Frank Zappa, Rick Beato’s YouTube podcasts, and books about Broadway musicals and Black opera innovators.

These disparate writings are among the recipients of the 77th annual ASCAP Foundation Deems Taylor/Virgil Thomson Awards, voted on by a select committee of four ASCAP members to recognize the best in books, articles, liner notes and broadcast programs about all forms of music.

Related Stories

Vino G. Bastian, Pevita Pearce, Faradina Mufti, Indra Jegel Lead 'Miracle in Cell No. 7' Director Lee Hwan-kyung’s Indonesian Father-Son Drama 'Gasigogi' (EXCLUSIVE)

Pedro Pascal on Learning Cello for ‘Behemoth!,’ Why ‘You’ve Got to Eat S---’ to Make It in Hollywood and the ‘Avengers: Doomsday’ Line His Character Says

The film composer biographies being recognized were Tim Greiving ‘s “John Williams: A Composer’s Life,” the first-ever biography about Hollywood’s most successful living composer, which got a Deems Taylor/Virgil Thomson Book Award in the field of concert music, and Steven C. Smith ‘s “Hitchcock and Herrmann: The Friendship and Film Scores that Changed Cinema,” the author’s second book about Herrmann (with a twist that makes it dually the story of his greatest filmmaker collaborator), which was given a special recognition award in the same category. (Both books were also on Variety ‘s list of the best music books of 2025 .)

Popular on Variety

Another book award in the concert music field, this one outside the realm of film music, went to Lucy Caplan for “Dreaming in Ensemble: How Black Artists Transformed American Opera.” Awards for books in the pop music field were given to Gayle Wald for “This Is Rhythm: Ella Jenkins, Children’s Music, and the Long Civil Rights Movement” and James O’Leary for The Middlebrow Musical: Between Broadway and Opera in 1940s America.”

Among the articles that won recognition from the ASCAP judges were a piece by the New York Times’ Ben Sisario about efforts to rescue decaying master tapes, a story by Esteban Meneses about Mexican symphonic composers and an article by the New York Times’ Max Keller about cellists debating the right way to hold their instruments. A piece in the Atlantic by Gabriel Kahana won for outstanding music criticism.

The top broadcast award went to Gail Wein for her podcast series “Classical Gas,” with a special recognition honor for Beato for his YouTube series “Everything Music.”

A liner notes award was given to percussionist Ruth Komanoff Underwood for her personal essay contained in the boxed set for “Cheaper than Cheep,” a live 1974 concert film by Frank Zappa and the Mothers of Invention.

A broadcast/media award in the pop field went to directors Isaac Gale, Ryan Olson and David McMurry for their documentary “Swamp Dogg Gets His Pool Painted.”

The judges for this year’s honors were Robbie Fulks, Julie Flanders, Carman Moore and Betsy Schramm.

The full list of winners, as provided by ASCAP:

The Deems Taylor/Virgil Thomson Broadcast/Media Award in pop music recognizes directors Isaac Gale, Ryan Olson and David McMurry for their documentary film “Swamp Dogg Gets His Pool Painted,” released in 2025, a unique storytelling of the legendary cult R&B musician Jerry “Swamp Dogg” Williams’s and his housemates’ musical creative life in Los Angeles surrounding his pool.

The Deems Taylor/Virgil Thomson Broadcast/Media Award in concert music recognizes radio host and producer Gail Wein for “Classical Gas,” produced by Classical Voice North America, the 2025 podcast series of interviews with classical musicians available on multiple platforms. A Special Recognition Award in the above category is given to Rick Beato for his 2025 YouTube series, “Everything Music,” exploring music, technology and issues facing music creators in today’s industry.

The ASCAP Foundation Paul Williams “Loved the Liner Notes” Award honors percussionist Ruth Komanoff Underwood for her personal essay for “Cheaper than Cheep,” the live box set from the 1974 concert film by Frank Zappa and The Mothers of Invention, on ZAPPA RECORDS/UMe.

The Deems Taylor/Virgil Thomson Book Awards in pop music are presented to: Gayle Wald for “This Is Rhythm: Ella Jenkins, Children’s Music, and the Long Civil Rights Movement,” the life story of “the first lady of children’s music,” published by University of Chicago Press. James O’Leary for “The Middlebrow Musical: Between Broadway and Opera in 1940s America,” an exploration of how musicals such as Oklahoma!, Beggar’s Holiday, and Street Scene embraced weighty stories in ways not seen before 1943, published by Oxford University Press.

The Deems Taylor/Virgil Thomson Book Awards in concert music go to: Lucy Caplan for “Dreaming in Ensemble: How Black Artists Transformed American Opera,” an account of Black innovation in American opera during the Harlem Renaissance, published by Harvard University Press. Tim Greiving for “John Williams: A Composer’s Life,” the first biography of one of the most important film composers of all time, published by Oxford University Press. Special Recognition Award in the above category is given to Steven C. Smith for “Hitchcock and Herrmann: The Friendship and Film Scores that Changed Cinema,” published by Oxford University Press.

The Deems Taylor/Virgil Thomson Award recipients for articles published in 2025 are as follows: The Deems Taylor/Virgil Thomson Award for an article in the pop music field goes to Ben Sisario, “The ‘Race Against Time’ to Save Music Legends’ Decaying Tapes,” on the intricate efforts to restore analog tapes with original recordings from Bruce Springsteen, Bob Dylan and more, published by The New York Times. The Deems Taylor/Virgil Thomson Award for an article in the concert music field goes to Esteban Meneses, “Revolución: Mexican Composers on the Rise,” a look at Mexican composers whose works are being performed, commissioned, and recorded by orchestras around the world, published by Symphony Magazine. Special Recognition Award in the above category is given to Max Keller, “Does It Matter How A Cello Is Held? It’s a Centuries-Old Debate,“ published by The New York Times.

The Virgil Thomson Award for Outstanding Music Criticism is presented to Gabriel Kahane for his article, “A Love Letter to Music Listings,” published by The Atlantic.

article_text:
シャネル・ネクサス・ホールにて、「Icons and Image Makers ナショナルポートレートギャラリー展」が開催される。

本展ではロンドンのナショナルポートレートギャラリーが所蔵する世界屈指の写真コレクションから、 英国のファッション、音楽、映画界を象徴するアイコンたちのポートレートを厳選して紹介。国際的に高い評価を受ける写真家たちの作品を通して、英国カルチャーを彩った人物像と、時代を映し出すポートレート写真の魅力に迫る。

ポートレートの中には、私たちの視覚文化に深く刻まれ、時代を象徴するイメージとなったものがある。その一方で、公のイメージの背後にある、一人の人間としての姿が捉えられたこともあった。こうした魅力的な肖像は、ナショナルポートレートギャラリーのコレクションの核心にある問いを投げかける。——イメージとアイデンティティはどこで交差するのか？——本展は、英国文化を牽引してきた アイコンたち、そして彼らの姿を形づくってきた写真家たちのクリエイティビティを称える展覧会である。

また会期初日には、ナショナルポートレートギャラリーのアシスタントキュレーターによるガイドイベントが開催されるなど、関連イベントも実施予定。この機会にぜひ足をお運びいただきたい。

article_text:
H ere is a disquieting documentary about what Israel’s military chiefs in Gaza reputedly call “Naza”, meaning civilian collateral damage – itself a queasy euphemism. The calculated “Naza” number is the amount of projected civilian deaths from each military strike, and perhaps it will come to have the same connotations as the US military term “body count” during Vietnam. The directors are Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, two of the film-makers behind No Other Land , which was about attacks by the Israel Defense Forces on Palestinian West Bank villages. NAZA is executive produced by Jonathan Glazer and James Wilson and appears under the production auspices of the Guardian, in which some of the stories have already appeared.

There are flaws: interviews were conducted on the condition of anonymity, but if no-one can be persuaded to put their name and face to their words (and of course it is terribly dangerous) then the impact of this as testimony is lessened. But even so, the film is casting a chilling light on what is happening now in Gaza .

Their faces in shadow, appearances and voices digitally altered, disillusioned Israeli intelligence officers and personnel speak to the directors about the war in Gaza. They do this semi-furtively on the dark night-time rooftops of Tel Aviv, the home of Israeli intelligence, supposedly for journalistic secrecy purposes – but it also provides a dramatic backdrop, as well as ambient footage of the city in all its eerie heedlessness and heartlessness. Periodically, the camera’s eye will drift across the gleaming apartment buildings, zooming in on glimpses of prosperous lives just 60km from Gaza.

The interviewees reject the whole concept of “human shields”. They allege that it is not a question of Hamas operatives hiding behind civilians; rather, Israel’s intelligence services have subcontracted their attack recon to AI. A computer program reportedly analyses the call pattern on phones belonging to known Hamas terrorists and finds which of the other tens of thousands of phones they have under surveillance exhibit the same tendencies – and then attack the owner, invariably at night, in the apartments whose whereabouts are already minutely documented by the state. A 15% permitted “error” rate for this is mentioned at one stage, and another respondent talks about an expected “Naza” rate of 20 for each action – but clearly this is elastic to say the least. Gaza’s civilians are considered to be all tacitly complicit in the grotesque antisemitic pogrom of 7 October, and whole buildings and vast numbers of people can be wiped out in one computer-generated assault.

Elsewhere, the officials talk about the logistics involved in “cleansing” northern Gaza and in sniper attacks on Gazan civilians who, desperate for food, don’t know they have crossed some invisible line into a militarised zone. Another part of the film talks about an intelligence unit unofficially loyal to prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu personally, engaging in dirty tricks undermining international human rights bodies who might be antipathetic to Israel’s political leadership.

The ahistorical comparison to nazism is inevitably and glibly invoked by one speaker. But Gaza, however horrendous, is not the same as the Holocaust. This specious parallel is all too readily available; the bombing of Dresden is the more obvious comparison. At all events, the anguish of Gaza is brought into pin-sharp focus.

article_text:
In 1995, Emma Thompson adapted Jane Austen’s novel into Ang Lee’s now-iconic film , “ Sense and Sensibility .” Thompson also played eldest sister Elinor Dashwood, with a rising Kate Winslet as her sister, Marianne, along with their love interests, Hugh Grant as Edward Ferrars and Alan Rickman as Colonel Brandon.

Now, 31 years later, a new movie adaptation , starring Daisy Edgar-Jones, Esmé Creed-Miles, Caitríona Balfe , George MacKay, Herbert Nordrum, and Fiona Shaw has arrived in theaters in appropriately high style. Diana Reid, author of “Seeing Other People,” wrote this adaptation of Austen’s 1811 novel.

To catch you up, here’s a helpful guide to everything you need to know about this new adaptation. Plus, we take a walk down memory lane to the 1995 version. And, director Georgia Oakley tell us what made each actor perfect for their role.

Marianne Dashwood

Esmé Creed-Miles

Esmé Creed-Miles’ Marianne has a jagged edge to her that tells us that she’s just getting started. Creed-Miles hails from acting royalty. Her mom’s a man-eater in “The Odyssey,” and not in that cute Hall & Oates way. Samantha Morton’s Circe really ate all the men.

Like mother, like daughter, Creed-Miles’ presence on screen is edgy, passionate, and vulnerable. Her Marianne has a darker undertone than previous Mariannes, and she has unique chemistry with both Frank Dillane, who plays Willoughby and Herbert Nordrum, who plays Colonel Brandon. You feel her pain when the former shuns her, and then you can’t look away when the latter gently longs for her. Watching two people fall in love when they don’t know they’re falling in love is timeless. Even in her most desperate moments, you can’t help but be captivated by her messy Marianne.

Oakley shared, “The first time she came to audition for us, she was wearing a ripped band t-shirt. She’d been on tour with her band. It was not what I was expecting at all. She’s able to have a command of Austen’s language that makes it sound like she’s just having a conversation with her mate. We always say that about great Shakespeare: If somebody’s doing it right, you don’t even notice the Shakespearean language. And I think Esme has an extraordinary ability to speak in Austen’s language.

1995: Kate Winslet. Before she almost sank on the Titanic and kicked off one of the greatest debates in film history, “Could Jack have fit on that piece of wood?” A virtually unknown young Kate Winslet played Marianne. It was hard to imagine the Dashwood sisters being anyone but Winslet and Thompson. Until now.

Elinor Dashwood

Daisy Edgar-Jones

Everyone fell in love with Edgar-Jones in “Normal People,” in which she played Marianne, star-crossed love of Paul Mescal’s Connell. And now, she takes over the Emma Thompson role of Elinor. Edgar-Jones’ chemistry with George MacKay, let’s just say they are the King and Queen of Yearning.

Oakley added, “It was amazing having her as our leader. She was guiding all of the other actors, and she has she has this kind of goofiness to her that is really interesting for Elinor because, yes, there’s that restraint, but there’s also there is a humor, and her and Edward in our version, they connect through a type of humor that she doesn’t share with the rest of her family, and that he doesn’t share with the rest of his family. It’s a combination of poise and humor that she brings.”

1995: Emma Thompson not only wrote the screenplay adaptation, but she won an Oscar for it. She played the unforgettable Elinor, who falls hopelessly in love with Hugh Grant’s Edward Ferrars. She and Grant would go on to star in four films together, sometimes as lovers and sometimes as siblings. She also met her husband filming “Sense and Sensibility.” You’ll find out who below.

Mrs. Dashwood

Caitríona Balfe

Hot off her decade long run as Claire Fraser in “Outlander,” Balfe pops on to the big screen with not one, but three movies that are out right now. Not escaping the curse of the corset, this was one of her first post-“Outlander” projects. She was quickly cast as Mrs. Dashwood, widow and mother to Marianne, Elinor, and Margaret.

Balfe confessed in an interview when she first got the role, she thought, “Surely, I’m not the mother.” Director Oakley soon pointed out she intentionally cast Mrs. Dashwood younger, since back in those days, women became mothers very young. In fact, Balfe’s Mrs. Dashwood is almost like the cool, older sister, that also happens to be their mother. We need to see young Mrs. Dashwood’s story. Perhaps a new Austen incarnation for the future: “The Dashwood Diaries.” Give us the goods.

Oakley added, “Oh, Caitríona, she’s just the loveliest person and such a talented actor. She brings a humor and something whimsical about Mrs. Dashwood. It says in the book that everybody falls in love with Mrs. Dashwood when they walk in into the cottage, and Caitríona was kind of the glue that held that family together.”

1995: Gemma Jones played mother Dashwood to Thompson and Winslet, but that’s not her most famous mother role. She played Bridget Jones’ mother as well. Now let’s imagine a “Bridget Jones’ Diary”/Dashwood time travel crossover. Bridget falls back in time and the Dashwoods adopt her.

Edward Ferrars

George MacKay

You’ll fall in love with George MacKay’s Edward Ferrars from the minute he first steps on screen and locks eyes with Edgar-Jones’ Elinor. Their instant yearn and burn fuels the film, and you can’t even be mad at him forgetting to mention he’s already engaged. Oops . His crinkly-eyed, smile wins over every Dashwood. Though Marianne calls him boring and generally is unimpressed with him, until she realizes how deeply smitten her usually unfazed sister is with him.

Oakley confessed, “George is Edward. We nicknamed Daisy and George head boy and head girl because they just had this very conscientious way of working, and they would always be doing something. They’d be sat on a fire escape running lines for like the scene that was coming up in two weeks.” Similar to his predecessor Grant, “Sense and Sensibility” should catapult MacKay into the romantic comedy lead for the foreseeable future.

1995: Hugh Grant plays the bumbling yet charming Ferrars, which would become his brand over the next 20 years. From “Four Weddings and a Funeral” to “Bridget Jones’ Diary” to “Two Weeks Notice,” Grant’s adorable romantic bumbler has won over Julia Roberts, Sandra Bullock, and many more on screen. But never forget, he once melted Emma Thompson’s Dashwood-en heart.

John Willoughby

Frank Dillane

Dillane’s Willoughby, like Creed-Miles’ Marianne, has more of a darkness lurking beneath. But he and Creed-Miles’ chemistry will hook you, just like it did with every Dashwood dame from the moment he scoops her up on that beach. So, when he courts, swoons, and ultimately ghosts Marianne, you will feel a mild rage toward him, and satisfaction when Colonel Brandon tosses him on out on his two-timing tucchus. Dillane played 16-year-old Tom Riddle in “Harry Potter,” and Nick Clark in “Fear of the Walking Dead.”

1995: Greg Wise’s Willoughby was cute to boot, and then gave Winslet’s Marianne the boot. But you know what, Wise got the girl in real life: He ended up with on-screen Elinor! As in, he’s Mr. Emma Thompson! Way to go Willoughby. Where there’s a Willoughby there’s way. Wise move. All puns intended.

Colonel Brandon

Herbert Nordrum

Nordrum plays Colonel Brandon as a sad, hopeless yet smoldering sleeper suitor who can’t take his eyes off of Marianne. On the other hand, Marianne goes out of her way to insult him for not being passionate about anything. Oh, how wrong she is. He spends most of the film being in love with her from afar, waiting patiently until she gets over her case of the Willoughby.

Oakley revealed that she actually didn’t think Nordrum was right for the role at first , because he’s so funny. “He’s just such a good-natured person,” she said. “There’s something kind of mysterious about him in the way that I had always read Brandon. He has a natural empathy. He sees the good in everybody. He’s a very generous actor.”

1995: Alan Rickman. He’s been Hans Gruber, Professor Snape, the man who cheated on Emma Thompson in one of the most re-watched Christmas movies of all-time, “Love Actually.” In “Sense and Sensibility,” he plays the seemingly boring Brandon, who locked onto Marianne long before she even remembered he was in the room. When re-watching this version, it will be hard not to hear hints of Hans Gruber. Rickman might be gone, but thankfully he lives on in every character of his we’re haunted by, scared of, and in this case, utterly and subtly charmed by.

Mrs. Jennings

Fiona Shaw

Fiona Shaw quite simply lights up every single scene she is in. She has chemistry with everyone, but most especially her co-star, the pug. Oakley revealed in an interview how she went the extra mile with her canine scene partner in one particular scene, and how it gloriously backfired. The scene with Shaw, Edgar-Jones, Balfe, and Creed-Miles watching Willoughby and Colonel Brandon fighting is one of funniest scenes in the entire film. Peak ensemble comedy.

1995: Elizabeth Spriggs won a BAFTA for her run as Mrs. Jennings.

John Dashwood

Tom Brooke

Tom Brooke brings awkward to a new hilarious level as Mrs. Dashwood’s stepson who inherits their house and fortune leaving them all penniless. His wife, Fanny, convinces him not to give them anything, even though it was his father’s dying wish. Without Fanny, John might actually have been a good brother and stepson, but “happy wife, happy life” was more his style, as he waved “ta-ta” to his half-sisters and stepmother. Brooke is currently starring in “Slow Horses.”

1995: James Fleet plays the weak Dashwood heir with a cluelessness that almost makes him endearing. Almost. Fleet appeared with Hugh Grant as Tom in “Four Weddings and a Funeral.”

Fanny Dashwood

Stacy Martin

Oh, Fanny. The Dashwood villain flies in on her little broom when the OG Mr. Dashwood dies. Martin brings a hilariously evil energy to the wife who can’t wait to kick her husband’s “half” family to the curb. When Mrs. Dashwood and her daughters move into their new smaller cottage, Mrs. Dashwood says, “Well, at least Fanny doesn’t live here.” Indeed. Martin plays her perfectly. Hard to believe Fanny and Edward came from the same family, as one is the blonde devil and the other is the sweetest man who just happened to forget to mention he’s engaged.

1995: Harriet Walter’s Fanny Dashwood is delightfully terrible. Walter is best known for her theater career with the Royal Shakespeare Company. She can now be seen on “Silo” with Rebecca Ferguson.

Margaret Dashwood

Bodhi Rae Breathnach

Breathnach plays the youngest Dashwood daughter, Margaret. Breathnach’s film debut was as William Shakespeare’s eldest daughter Susannah in Chloe Zhao’s “Hamnet.” As Margaret, Breathnach provides unfiltered, childlike candor with a sense of humor to boot. Young Dashwood often drops bangers like, “He won’t visit, that’s just what men say.” But she’s an Elinor and Edward stan from the very beginning.

1995: Emilie Francois played Margaret and went on to be a journalist, filmmaker, and writer.

“Sense and Sensibility” is in theaters now.

article_text:
In the hands of a director who loves his characters, the term “spare” to describe the style of a film should in no way imply a lack of warmth. On the contrary, minimalism can contain the essence of a story which might otherwise be constricted when set in a more distracting, less generously proportioned framework. Such is the case with Mohammed Hammad ’s virtuosic control of style and subject in “ Safe Exit ,” his long-awaited sophomore feature that premiered in the Berlinale’s Panorama program earlier this year. Rigorous in form without sacrificing its emotional power, the film addresses outsider status and the fear of terrorism in contemporary Cairo, proving that Hammad’s confident grasp, evident in his 2016 debut “Withered Green,” is the real deal.

On the outside, the challenges were great. The Christian male protagonist Samaan (Marwan Waleed) is a socially awkward young man traumatized by a terrorist incident that led to his father’s murder. Hampered by his inability to express himself, he records his thoughts in a journal heard in voice-over; the device could easily have been exposition-heavy, yet Hammad’s ultra-tight script avoids any feeling of didacticism. Instead, it concisely reveals Samaan’s ordeal when younger of being kidnapped by ISIS terrorists in Libya together with other Coptic families, and the survival guilt he lives with when he was let go.

Samaan works the night shift as a security guard in an apartment building that, like so many similar buildings in Cairo, is a microcosm of class and economic disparity — in which a coldly unpleasant lobby gives no sense of either the well-maintained apartments nor the rabbit-warren of illegal constructions on the roof where the young man lives. Needing to pay a lawyer to help his brother in detention following an altercation, Samaan makes a deal with a resident (Magda Mounir) hiding her terrorist son Abdullah (Hazem Essam) in her home, by which Samaan signals the arrival of police so the guy can hide in a rooftop water-tank when the building is being searched.

An on-site doctor’s office draws Fatimah (Noha Foad), an undocumented, illiterate Muslim woman suffering from seizures. Discovering that charity cases are only seen the following day, she gives herself to daytime security guard Amm Araby (Samer Al Miniawy), hoping for a place to sleep the night, but the guy chases her away afterwards and Samaan reluctantly allows her to stay over. Whereas Samaan is almost pathologically unassertive, Fatimah knows how to work her smile as well as her body, covering stark vulnerability with a flinty sense of self-protection.

Director-writer Hammad subtly adds layers to each character, refusing to allow either one to be reduced to mere victimhood. Samaan has written a novel — revealingly titled “Who Am I?” — which he hopes to get published, only to discover that the publisher charges production costs to the author. Fatimah’s seizures are diagnosed as symptoms of an operable brain tumor, but with no papers (despite being Egyptian), she’s ineligible for state-sponsored healthcare. The hesitant, unexpected rapport that develops between these two marginalized people holds out the hope of redemption, only to be dashed in a moment of panic mixed with blind cruelty.

Every scene is meticulously constructed (the storyboards could make an exhibition on their own), with Mohammed El Sharqawy’s camera remaining fixed apart from occasional slow zooms and a moment when hope itself seems to prompt a gentle movement, when Fatimah tells Samaan that a medallion of the Virgin Mary she nicked from him has become a good luck charm. Though his apartment has a garish flashing picture of Mary, he admits to not being a believer; one senses the decoration is a holdover from when his father was alive and it was still possible to trust in the prospect of supernatural protection.

There’s a beauty in watching the two lead actors together, each attuned to their character’s distinct kind of physicality. For relative newcomer Marwan Waleed, that means tense body movements and a downcast tilt to his head, reflecting the psychological toll of having been trapped in a locked van when kidnapped in Libya. Noha Foad, swathed in sober black that she manages to make both restrained and borderline provocative, equally inhabits her role, her movements discreetly sensuous when she knows she’s being watched. Her fragile command of every scene befits the character, never more so than in a close-up as she berates the Virgin for abandoning her: a Muslim, talking to the Christian divine mother, searching for hope. It’s a great testament to Waleed’s talents that his more interior projection holds his own alongside Foad’s unassailable warmth.

The title is unsurprisingly a misnomer, as there is no safe exit to be found. Hammad’s favored way of shooting interiors involves obliquely positioned walls where we see two rooms at the same time, each studiously lit with strong directional illumination emphasizing the darkness outside the luminous beams. Unexpectedly bright colors in Samaan’s apartment, with its views over Cairo, offer tantalizing prospects of a better tomorrow which fail to arrive. No wonder the Egyptian censors have so far only allowed the film to be screened at the El Gouna Film Festival.

Variety Awards Circuit section is the home for all awards news and related content throughout the year, featuring the following: the official predictions for the upcoming Oscars , Emmys , Grammys and Tony Awards ceremonies, curated by Variety chief awards editor Clayton Davis. The prediction pages reflect the current standings in the race and do not reflect personal preferences for any individual contender. As other formal (and informal) polls suggest, competitions are fluid and subject to change based on buzz and events. Predictions are updated every Thursday.

2027 Academy Awards Predictions Commentary All Categories (Updated: Oct. 22, 2026): Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s A24 documentary “You Can See Everything,” which follows the Theranos founder through the 34 days before she reported to prison and keeps rolling afterward, opened to a staggering $15 million over the weekend, a number most nonfiction films never see in a full run. It’s also boasting a record-setting 99 on Metacritic, 98% on Rotten Tomatoes and holding a 4.7 (out of 5) on Letterboxd and 9.4 on IMDb.

What if the first documentary nominated for best picture goes all the way to the top prize?

A few studios are trying to frame the race as David vs. Goliath regarding how they can possibly topple Christopher Nolan’s billion-dollar sensation “The Odyssey.” What if this is actually Odysseus vs. Elizabeth Holmes?

In addition to being eligible for best documentary feature at the 99th Academy Awards, the film will also be submitted across the board as seen on A24’s awards site: best picture (Nathan Fielder, Lance Oppenheim, Tatiana Bears, Maggie Ambrose and Jack Davis), director (Fielder and Oppenheim), production design (Alex DiGerlando and Rebecca Meis), cinematography (David Bolen), costume design (Katina Danabassis), film editing (Adam Locke-Norton), makeup and hairstyling (Stephanie Pasicov and Kerrie Smith), sound (Paul Hsu and Richard Carlos) and original score (Ari Balouzian).

Variety confirmed exclusively after the film made its surprise world premiere (and general existence became known) at the Telluride Film Festival that Amanda Seyfried, credited in the film as Elizabeth Holmes, is eligible for the Academy Awards in the acting categories. Seyfried, who also appears as herself while reprising her Emmy-winning turn as Holmes from “The Dropout,” will be campaigned in the supporting actress category. If she lands the nomination, it would be her second, following “Mank” (2020). She would get there for playing two people at once: herself and the woman she already won an Emmy statue for playing. Christopher Abbott, who also appears in the film as Holmes’ spouse, Billy Evans, in recreated scenes, is also eligible for acting consideration in the supporting actor category. Fielder, credited as himself, may be eligible to submit as a performer, but Variety has confirmed he won’t.

No documentary has ever been nominated for best picture in 98 ceremonies. The zeitgeist says this one can be.

The race is getting very exciting.

In other news, Variety has confirmed that Lionsgate’s bid to have its Michael Jackson biopic compete as a comedy or musical at the Golden Globes has been denied. The Golden Globes’ decision means the film, starring Jaafar Jackson as the King of Pop, is currently slated for the drama categories where it would compete for one of the six available slots against Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey,” Los Javis’ “La Bola Negra” and more. The supporting actor and actress categories do not separate by genre, so this has no effect on his co-stars Colman Domingo and Nia Long.

This week’s updates are below.

The Governors Awards, which will hand out honorary Oscars to Glenn Close and Ridley Scott, will take place Sunday, Nov. 15. Preliminary voting for the Oscars shortlist in 12 categories runs Dec. 7-11, with the shortlist announcement to follow Tuesday, Dec. 15. Following the close of the eligibility period on Dec. 31, 2026, nominations voting will run Jan. 11-15, 2027. The official Oscar nominations will be announced on Thursday, Jan. 21, 2027. The 99th Oscars will take place on Sunday, March 14, 2027 and will be hosted by Conan O’Brien. The ceremony airs live at 7 p.m. ET on ABC and in more than 200 territories worldwide from the Dolby Theatre at Ovation Hollywood.

EXCLUSIVE: The Studio breakout Chase Sui Wonders is in talks to join Goblin , A24 ’s new film from David Mikalson, which goes into production before end of year.

Character details are being kept under wraps. Wonders joins a cast that includes Kenneth Branagh, voicing the titular Goblin, along with Skyler Gisondo and Will Forte. Previously, we reported that the film is a raunchy comedy in the vein of Ted meets E.T.

Sui Wonders is coming off of the first season of the hit Apple series The Studio , where she plays assistant-turned-executive Quinn Hackett. Her work there earned her a Gotham TV Award nomination; Season 2 of The Studio airs next year.

Currently, Sui Wonders is in production opposite Jennifer Aniston, Peter Dinklage and her The Studio co-star Ike Barinholz on Universal’s holiday comedy Naughty from director Olivia Wilde. Next up, she’ll be seen in A24’s Slayground , an action thriller written and directed by Jeremy Saulnier, which releases on January 29, 2027. She is represented by UTA and Sloane Offer Weber & Dern.

From Hendrix to Bowie: the trippiest music concert posters – in pictures

Günther Kieser is behind some of the most singular music poster designs of the 20th century. Inspired by sculpture, the free-form nature of jazz and psychedelic art, the German artist created works for David Bowie, Jimi Hendrix and Diana Ross and the Supremes, as well as mind-expanding designs for leading brands and art institutions. The exhibition Sculpting Sound: Günther Kieser’s Music Posters at New York’s Poster House gallery showcases his decades-spanning work and runs from 12 November to 11 April 2027. article_text:
News

Para Site Announces Departure from Quarry Bay Location

Hong Kong’s Para Site is departing its location in Quarry Bay, where it has been based for a decade. On the occasion of its 30th anniversary, the nonprofit will embark on what it describes as a “nomadic” program that will unfold across the city throughout 2027.

In June, Para Site began its experimental, collaborative program “Elsewhere in Me” across Hong Kong, which will continue to showcase new commissions by local and international figures such as Sydney-based artist Justin Talplacido Shoulder (Phasmahammer) in November and Hong Kong-based artist Yim Sui Fong in December. The initiative part will continue into the new year while Para Site furnishes its new venue, which is yet to be announced.

Para Site was founded in 1996 by Hong Kong artists Patrick Lee, Leung Chi-wo, Phoebe Man Ching-ying, Sara Wong Chi-hang, Leung Mee-ping, Tsang Tak-ping, and Lisa Cheung as an alternative platform for nurturing discourse on contemporary art and collaborations between curators and creatives. Originally based in Sheung Wan, Para Site relocated to Quarry Bay in 2015.

James Taylor-Foster, who joined the institution as its executive director in March, told South China Morning Post that the year-long program is an opportunity to “try things out”: new ideas, partnerships, and relationships. “All this will inform the kind of space that we end up moving into—a new anchor point for Para Site in Hong Kong.”

Harison Butler is an editorial intern at ArtAsiaPacific.

article_text:
The artist’s first institutional solo in his native Indonesia for three decades is most enchanting when it speaks for itself

Three decades after he emigrated to Australia, Jumaadi’s first institutional solo exhibition in his native Indonesia gathers recent drawings, paintings, installations and a performance (the latter happens on three occasions, but is also available as a recording). In a dark screening-room lined with paper cutouts, a two-channel black-andwhite projection Laut Masih Menjadi Misteri (The Sea is Still a Mystery, 2023) shows a shadow-play set in a maritime environment: fishing boats, gigantic crustaceans, odd plants. Mounted nearby is a monitor concurrently playing behind-the-scenes footage: the artist moves the puppets closer to the lamp then sneaks them out of the screen, their silhouettes turning blurry to provide the illusion of distance. Right outside the screening room, storyboards are drawn on pleated papers and encased in a glass box. But however much the exhibition attempts to steer visitors into seeing how the sausage gets made, so to speak, the play is at its most enchanting when its primary elements – light and shadow – speak for themselves.

Alongside paintings made in acrylic on cloth, Jumaadi’s practice often draws on the traditional art of wayang kulit , or shadow puppetry – featuring characters with exaggerated features, generally presented in the side profile – to explore human relationships and natural cycles. For the exhibition’s centerpiece Orang Terkasih dan Bayang Bayangnya Abadi (The Eternal Shadows of Loved Ones, 2025–26), rows of 147 buffalo-hide cutouts (the traditional form of wayang-kulit puppets) depicting a cast of colourful characters are strung between the pillars of a wooden hut. The shadows of these inhabitants, cast on the wall, intermingle, suggesting a complex social constellation, one that is populated by people in domestic relationships (such as husband–wife or parent–child pairs) and chimeric creatures (such as humans with twin crocodile heads or others enveloped by fiery red snakes) alike.

Further up on the museum’s mezzanine floor, 13 intricately carved buffalo hides hang suspended from the ceiling. Each depicts myriad scenes at once. Take Sepasang Malaikat #2 (A Pair of Angels, 2026), an oval-shaped hide, painted in acrylic, in which the titular dyad takes centre stage, with each winged creature, one male, one female, swooping in to smooch the other as both spread their wings. A fringe of cutouts of tiny humans holding hands (as do the central angels) makes up the puppet’s perimeter. Motifs of waves, and trees with fetuses for roots, flood the rest of the surface area. Like all the works here, Sepasang Malaikat #2 can be observed recto verso, though all are hung close to the walls, perhaps to make clear that the most elegant standpoint remains the one that allows visitors to see (in this case) the painted work and its shadow imprinted on the wall behind it.

The exhibition demonstrates Jumaadi’s versatile take on the traditional artform as he deploys it to represent his original and inventive cosmological visions in which physical and spiritual realms intermingle. This is evident in Kaki Langit (The Sky’s Feet, 2026), in which a foot-shaped puppet depicts the human journey from life to death: nodal root systems inhabited by a curled-up body fill the puppet’s toes and heel, while a larger body, lying head down, and an array of skulls occupy the sole. Surrounding the rest of the foot are repetitive engravings of plants, birds and circular patterns; nature abounds from womb to tomb.

Jumaadi: Yang Bersayap Rangka Daun (The Winged One with the Skeleton of a Leaf) is on view at Tumurun Museum, Surakarta, through 10 January

article_text:
Hundred Heroines, devoted to promoting and championing women photographers, begins with an observation that has long gone unaddressed: behind the greatest portraits of twentieth-century stars, there was almost always a woman behind the lens. Its ambition is to restore these women to the centre of photographic history — a history they helped write, from which they have too often been erased.

For the earliest works in the show, Hundred Heroines has partnered with Sisters of the Lens, an organisation dedicated to promoting women photographers who worked between the 1850s and 1960s, which has made rare original prints available for this exhibition.

Three unjustly forgotten pioneers are brought back into the light: Lallie Charles, an Irish photographer based in London and one of the most celebrated society portraitists of the Edwardian era: Dorothy Wilding, the first woman appointed as Official Royal Photographer to the British Crown, whose portraits of Elizabeth II appeared on UK postage stamps; and Madame D’Ora, an Austrian photographer who established herself first in Vienna, then in Paris from 1925 onwards, as one of the defining portraitists of fashion and high society in the first half of the twentieth century.

These pioneers immortalized, among others, the British actress Vivien Leigh, whom the world first encountered in Gone with the Wind (1939), the blazing American entertainer Tallulah Bankhead, and the German-American star Marlene Dietrich, the supreme icon of pre-war cinema.

South African photographer Jillian Edelstein, born in Cape Town and based in London since the 1980s, dominates the contemporary section of the exhibition. Trained in photojournalism and published in the New York Times Magazine and Vogue , she pursues in every portrait “the humanity behind the mask of celebrity, the person behind the persona.”

Among Edelstein’s most powerful images is her portrait of the late British punk fashion designer Vivienne Westwood, who died in 2022, shot with her wild flame-orange hair and two small silver horns tucked into her curls, her expression poised somewhere between mischief and majesty. Amy Winehouse, the prodigiously gifted British soul and jazz singer who died at 27 in 2011, appears with arms folded and gaze averted — at once an icon and a raw, exposed soul.

The archive of Elisabeth Buchmeyer-Lewis, a British photographer specializing in the music world of the late twentieth century, provides an electric counterpoint. Her images plunge into the backstage world of British rock and jazz of the 1970s and 1980s: Ian Dury, singer, lyricist and founder of the Blockheads, hunched over his microphone at the legendary 100 Club on Oxford Street, alongside previously unseen photographs of American singer-songwriter Bob Dylan and British hard rock band Led Zeppelin, captured at close range from the stage. Taken together, these portraits measure the full extent of what women photographers gave to pop culture, and to the century that consumed it. “Stardust” puts the record straight.

“Stardust: 100 Years of Stage, Screen and Celebrity” by Hundred Heroines is on view at the new Hundred Heroines Photo Museum in Nailsworth, Gloucestershire, UK, from 11 September to 20 November 2026. Free admission.

Source: Courtesy of Sundance Institute

Tracy Brady

Sundance Institute has appointed Tracy Brady as chief marketing, brand and communications officer as the film festival prepares to relocate to Colorado for its first edition running January 21-31, 2027.

Brady is tasked with unifying the organisation’s messaging and public presence and tying together the Institute’s impact, artist programmes and upcoming Sundance Film Festival. She will be based in Boulder and reports to Sundance Institute CEO David Linde.

The executive most recently served as SVP of communications and social impact at the cannabis retailer Green Thumb Industries, and prior to that built the global communications team at the publicly-traded medical and recreational dispensary Curaleaf.

She has held roles in publicity, awards and marketing strategy at Sony Pictures Entertainment, the former Fox Searchlight Pictures, Turner Broadcasting and agencies including time as SVP of corporate communications and marketing at Hill Holiday, where she directed sponsorship and experiential marketing strategies for the Sundance Film Festival and other key clients. She has also advised CEOs, executive leadership and boards during organisational transformation and growth.

Linde called Brady “a visionary, strategic and results-oriented marketing and communications leader”, adding: “Tracy’s understanding of storytelling, brand marketing and strategic communications, coupled with her lifelong passion and dedication to the arts, makes her the perfect executive to guide our brand forward.”

“As we move toward the 2027 Sundance Film Festival in Boulder, my focus will be on bringing our entire community together, both inside the Institute and out,” Brady said.

article_text:
The Rouen Normandie Photography Centre and Le Point du Jour, an art centre and publisher (Cherbourg-en-Cotentin), in partnership with Cadre en Seine and l’Artothèque, Espaces d’art contemporain de Caen, are renewing the ‘50 cc Air de Normandie’ grant to support photographic creation in Normandy.

Aimed at professional photographers and artists who work primarily with photography and are resident in Normandy, it aims to support an ongoing project whose content is not restricted to any particular genre or geographical scope.

Since 2024, the grant has been awarded over two years, with an emphasis on research, networking and production. It comprises the following: – A research and creation grant of €8,000 (including VAT) over two years (€4,000 per year), awarded by the Centre Photographique Rouen Normandie and Le Point du Jour; – A material grant from Cadre en Seine (advice, printing, framing), amounting to €8,000 (excluding VAT) over two years (€4,000 per year); – Acquisition of one work by the Artothèque de Caen, up to a value of €2,000; – Project support through regular meetings with the management teams of the Centre photographique Rouen Normandie and Le Point du Jour; – Support for greater integration into the contemporary art scene through professional meetings with external figures, organised at the Carré Bisson / Cadre en Seine, Paris.
